cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed dismissal of a father's malpractice claim, holding that a health care professional whose treatment of a child patient produced allegations of sexual abuse owes no duty of care to the accused third party, and reasoning that Maine's mandated-reporter scheme makes negligent reporting non-actionable.
cases.quote: Negligent reporting is not actionable.

relevance.INP-01: This is the Law Court's statement of the liability shield behind 22 M.R.S. §§ 4011-A and 4014 for professionals who must report suspected abuse, so a mandated reporter faces no negligence exposure for a good-faith report.
relevance.INP-02: The same immunity reasoning protects any person who reports in good faith, which is what makes the voluntary-report channel usable without fear of a retaliatory suit.
relevance.INP-06: Because negligent reporting is not actionable, a hotline or anonymous caller reporting in good faith cannot be sued by the person named in the report.
relevance.INP-07: The case arose from a health care provider's treatment and reporting of suspected sexual abuse and is the leading Maine authority on the absence of a duty running from clinicians to accused third parties.
relevance.INP-08: School and other professional reporters take the same protection: the Court refused to create a duty that would deter detection and reporting of abuse.

cases.case_name: Seider v. Board of Examiners of Psychologists
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed professional discipline of a psychologist who, in responding to a child-protective investigative subpoena, disclosed confidential client information far beyond what the subpoena requested, and held her statutory-immunity argument unpreserved because it was not raised before the Board.
cases.quote: The Board did not err in finding that Seider violated Principle 5.02 of the APA Code.

relevance.INP-01: A mandated reporter's duty is to report immediately, but the Court held that the reporter's disclosure obligation does not license unlimited disclosure of confidential client material.
relevance.INP-07: For clinicians making a medical or mental-health disclosure, this case marks the outer limit: information supplied to the Department must be germane to the child-protective purpose.
relevance.DEC-02: During the Department's investigation the psychologist responded to an investigative subpoena under 22 M.R.S. § 4021; the Court held that immunity does not excuse disclosures exceeding the subpoena's scope.
relevance.FAIL-06: The decision shows the flip side of a transparency failure: over-disclosure of confidential child-protective material is itself sanctionable.

cases.holding: The Law Court vacated termination of the father's parental rights because, without a rehabilitation and reunification plan establishing the services he was required to complete, his failure to abstain from alcohol and complete counseling could not establish unfitness by clear and convincing evidence, and vacated as to the mother so her unfitness and best-interest determinations could be reconsidered.
cases.quote: Unless the Department has been excused from reunification efforts, the rehabilitation and reunification plan is the centerpiece of child protective proceedings following a jeopardy determination.

relevance.ACT-01: The Court describes the plan as the instrument through which services are agreed and measured, so a purely voluntary service arrangement that is never memorialized in a plan cannot later be used as a benchmark against the parent.
relevance.ACT-02: This is Maine's leading authority on court-ordered service plans under 22 M.R.S. § 4041: the Department must develop the plan when the child enters foster care and the court must resolve disputes about its contents.
relevance.DEC-04: The removal here proceeded by ex parte preliminary protection order followed by a waived summary preliminary hearing, and the Court measured the sixty-day foster-care entry clock from that removal.
relevance.DEC-06: Because the plan is the centerpiece of post-jeopardy practice, a non-adjudicatory or service-only track that produces no written plan leaves the agency without a measurable benchmark.
relevance.INP-12: The opinion traces the path from emergency protective custody through ex parte preliminary protection order to jeopardy, fixing the date a child is deemed to have entered foster care.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification in Maine runs through the statutory plan, and the Department's failure to finalize one is an important factor weighing against a later termination petition.

cases.case_name: John Doe v. Department of Health and Human Services
cases.holding: The Law Court held that the Department's unpromulgated 2000 policy created no judicially enforceable appeal deadline and that denying Doe any hearing to contest his 2003 substantiation violated procedural due process, and it remanded for the Department to provide him an administrative review and hearing.
cases.quote: Thus, all three Mathews factors, as applied to this case, weigh in favor of Doe and against the Department.

relevance.DEC-01: The Court's Mathews analysis rests on the very high rate at which appealed substantiations were overturned, which is direct evidence that front-end screening and closure decisions carry a real risk of error.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the controlling Maine authority that a substantiated finding triggers a due-process right to notice of the collateral consequences and to a hearing before an impartial factfinder.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the clearest modern example of a Maine court reversing an agency's refusal to review its own child-abuse finding.
relevance.FAIL-06: The Department's failure to tell Doe what a substantiation would cost him was itself a constitutional disclosure failure.
relevance.INP-10: An intake that escalates to investigation and substantiation must carry with it a promulgated, APA-compliant appeal procedure, not an internal policy.
relevance.PMC-05: An agency policy that was never adopted under the Administrative Procedure Act is void and unenforceable, a point that matters whenever a state claims an unpublished rule bars review.

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed a jeopardy order and accompanying cease-reunification order entered against a non-resident father, holding that a Maine court needs only that the child reside or be present in Maine and need not have personal jurisdiction over a parent to adjudicate jeopardy and order a disposition.
cases.quote: None of the determinations that a court is called upon to make in a jeopardy proceeding requires the court to have personal jurisdiction over a parent.

relevance.ACT-03: The Court confirmed that placing the child in the Department's custody is part of the jeopardy disposition the court may order even as to an out-of-state parent.
relevance.ACT-05: The jeopardy order operated as the protective disposition, including a cease-reunification provision, under 22 M.R.S. § 4036.
relevance.DEC-04: The decision identifies the statutory predicate for judicial protective action as a finding that the child is in circumstances of jeopardy, not the parent's amenability to suit.
relevance.DEC-05: Venue for a child protection petition lies where the child resides or is present, and service of the petition on a parent under 22 M.R.S. § 4033(1)(A) is all the statute requires.
relevance.INP-04: The case shows how a court acquires and exercises child-protection jurisdiction once a petition is filed, regardless of a parent's location.
relevance.INP-12: Emergency and protective determinations focus on the child's circumstances, which is why the child's presence in Maine is the jurisdictional anchor.

cases.case_name: In re Children of Bethmarie R.
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed a jeopardy order and an order directing the Department to cease reunification based on the aggravating factor of heinous or abhorrent treatment, rejecting the mother's due process challenge founded on a contemporaneous Probate Court guardianship proceeding that had reached a different result on overlapping evidence.
cases.quote: No due process violation has been demonstrated on this record.

relevance.ACT-02: The opinion sets out how an aggravating-factor finding under 22 M.R.S. § 4002(1-B) relieves the Department of the service and reunification obligations that would otherwise drive the case plan.
relevance.ACT-05: The District Court's jeopardy order was the protective instrument, and it displaced the Probate Court's transitional-services order for the same children.
relevance.DEC-05: The decision is a caution that the District Court's exclusive child-protection jurisdiction and the Probate Court's guardianship jurisdiction can run in parallel over the same children.
relevance.INP-04: A pending Probate Court guardianship proceeding is a common referral pathway into a District Court child protection petition, and this case shows both moving at once.
relevance.OUT-01: Where an aggravating factor is found, reunification is not the default outcome and the permanency plan may move directly to termination.

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed the jeopardy order, holding that the aggravating-factor finding embedded in a jeopardy order may be reviewed for evidentiary sufficiency but that the resulting cease-reunification order is interlocutory and not itself subject to appellate review, overruling contrary suggestions in earlier cases.
cases.quote: In some limited circumstances, however, the court may relieve the Department of those efforts by issuing a cease reunification order.

relevance.ACT-02: This is the Maine authority defining when a court may relieve the Department of its statutory rehabilitation and reunification obligations under 22 M.R.S. § 4041(2)(A-2).
relevance.DEC-06: It marks the point at which the case leaves the service-and-reunification track entirely, so any alternative-response posture ends once an aggravating factor is found.
relevance.OUT-01: A parent who wants to preserve reunification must attack the factual finding of an aggravating factor, because the cease-reunification disposition itself is unreviewable on appeal.

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed jeopardy findings made by a preponderance of the evidence, reached the merits under the collateral-consequences exception because a jeopardy finding can generate an administrative substantiation, and clarified that a trial court may dismiss a child protection petition under 22 M.R.S. § 4036(1-A) while an appeal from the jeopardy order is pending.
cases.quote: A finding that children are in circumstances of jeopardy must be supported by a preponderance of the evidence.

relevance.DEC-05: This states the burden of proof that governs the adjudicatory hearing once the Department files its petition, and the clear-error standard on review.
relevance.OUT-04: The Court reached the merits of a jeopardy appeal notwithstanding the child's age, applying the collateral-consequences exception recognized where a child had turned eighteen during the appeal.
relevance.OUT-05: The opinion confirms that the trial court may dismiss the petition when entry of a parental rights order will alleviate jeopardy, even while an appeal is pending.

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed terminations entered in private adoption proceedings, holding that neither due process nor equal protection requires a court in a title 18-A private termination and adoption case to order the rehabilitation and reunification services that would be available in a title 22 Department case.
cases.quote: In summary, the court was not constitutionally required by the Due Process Clause to order the provision of any particular services in the private adoption proceeding.

relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary or agency-funded services are a statutory benefit tied to Department involvement, not a constitutional entitlement a parent can demand in a private case.
relevance.DEC-06: Where no petition is filed by the Department, the front-end service pathway simply does not exist, and the Constitution does not supply one.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the controlling Maine authority distinguishing the procedural protections owed in Department-initiated terminations from those in private termination and adoption proceedings.

cases.holding: In Maine's first ICWA case the Law Court affirmed termination of parental rights to Maliseet children, holding that the active-efforts element of 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) must be proved by clear and convincing evidence but does not oblige the agency to persist in futile efforts.
cases.quote: we cannot say that the federal guidelines contained in the Indian Children Welfare Act required the DHS to engage in futile, nonproductive efforts to reunify this Indian family

relevance.INP-11: This is the foundational Maine decision applying ICWA's heightened active-efforts standard to an Indian child, and it fixes clear and convincing evidence as the state-law proof standard for that element.
relevance.OUT-01: It defines the outer limit of the agency's reunification duty where a parent with limited capacity or a refusing parent makes further services pointless, while still requiring proof that efforts were actually made.

cases.case_name: In re Child of Radience K.
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination of parental rights to an Indian child, holding that ICWA adds to state law an active-efforts element provable by clear and convincing evidence and a beyond-a-reasonable-doubt finding of likely serious emotional or physical damage, and that both were satisfied on this record.
cases.quote: ICWA imposes two elements of proof in a state court termination proceeding beyond those required by state law.

relevance.INP-11: This is the modern Maine synthesis of the combined state and ICWA burdens once a case is identified as involving an Indian child, including tribal notice and the tribe's designated qualified expert witness.

cases.holding: The Law Court held that appointing a guardian for a minor over a parent's objection on the de facto guardian provision's preponderance standard violates procedural due process, construed the statute to require clear and convincing evidence, and vacated and remanded for application of that standard.
cases.quote: Notwithstanding the plain language of section 5-204(d), the applicable standard of proof must be proof by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.INP-05: When a relative or caregiver petitions for guardianship instead of calling the hotline, the parent is constitutionally entitled to the clear and convincing standard before losing custody.
relevance.OUT-03: This is the controlling Maine constitutional decision on the burden of proof for establishing a minor guardianship as a permanency route over a parent's objection.

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed denial of a mother's motion to open her termination proceeding to the public, holding that 22 M.R.S. § 4007(1) presumptively closes child protection proceedings and records and that the mother lacked standing to assert the public's First Amendment right of access.
cases.quote: the Legislature intended section 4007(1) to mean that child protection proceedings are presumptively closed

relevance.FAIL-04: The case arose after the mother's other daughter died in the foster home the Department had selected and the foster mother was criminally charged, and the Court still held the protective proceeding presumptively closed.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the leading Maine authority for the proposition that closure is the default, so a transparency claim must identify a specific statutory or regulatory exception.
relevance.INP-09: Public and legislative scrutiny following a death in care does not by itself open the underlying case file.
relevance.OUT-06: The decision arises directly from a child fatality in foster care and shows what the surviving sibling's proceeding looks like afterwards.
relevance.PMC-03: Any citizen-review or oversight body seeking case-level material in Maine must work within the narrow disclosure exceptions in 22 M.R.S. §§ 4007-4009.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality review of a death in care runs up against the presumption of closure recognized here, and the Court tied that presumption to CAPTA's confidentiality conditions at 42 U.S.C. § 5106a(b)(4).
relevance.PMC-05: A court may disclose confidential child-protective information only when disclosure is necessary to resolve an issue pending before it under 22 M.R.S. § 4008(3).

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed summary judgment for two Department caseworkers, holding that their decisions about how much of a child's sexual-abuse history to disclose to relatives seeking his placement were discretionary functions absolutely immune under 14 M.R.S.A. § 8111(1)(C), even assuming negligence or bad faith.
cases.quote: The Legislature has immunized from suit caseworkers' discretionary actions within the scope of their employment.

relevance.ACT-03: Placement decisions and the information shared about a placed child fall inside the discretionary-function immunity, which sharply limits tort remedies for a bad placement.
relevance.ACT-04: The relatives who took the child in had no tort remedy when the caseworkers withheld his history, which is the practical risk kinship caregivers assume in Maine.
relevance.FAIL-02: The case marks the boundary of caseworker liability in Maine tort law: discretionary conduct within the scope of employment is immune, so most claims must be pleaded as constitutional claims under § 1983.
relevance.FAIL-04: Where a child is harmed in a placement the agency arranged, Maine Tort Claims Act immunity will usually defeat the negligence theory.
relevance.OUT-06: Serious injury to a child following an agency placement decision does not defeat discretionary immunity, even on allegations of intentional misrepresentation.

cases.case_name: In re Children of Matthew G.
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights, holding the court did not rest its unfitness finding impermissibly on his incarceration and denying his ineffective-assistance claim because he filed no supporting affidavit.
cases.quote: the court did not impermissibly consider the father's incarceration in reaching its parental unfitness determination, and therefore it did not err in finding that the father is unfit

relevance.OUT-02: This is the Maine rule for incarcerated parents: incarceration is not a standalone ground, but a parent who cannot meet the child's needs now and in the foreseeable future is unfit whatever the cause.

cases.case_name: In re Child of Stephen E.
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination, holding the father failed to make a prima facie showing of ineffective assistance where his counsel withdrew two months before the hearing and he never requested substitute counsel, a continuance, or responded to court notices.
cases.quote: The father's claim of ineffective assistance is not persuasive when, like the reunification process, he was a nonparticipant in the judicial process.

relevance.FAIL-01: It sets the substantive bar for overturning a termination on ineffective-assistance grounds and confirms that a signed, sworn affidavit stating the basis of the claim with specificity is mandatory.

cases.case_name: Kane v. Commissioner of Department of Health & Human Services
cases.holding: The Law Court vacated the Commissioner's substantiation of a foster parent for abuse and neglect, holding that because a substantiation carries life-altering consequences and implicates a fundamental liberty interest, it requires proof of something more than imperfect or deficient parenting.
cases.quote: a substantiation finding must be based on an understanding that "abuse or neglect" means, for purposes of section 4088(3)(K), something more than imperfect, overly rigid, or even deficient parenting

relevance.ACT-06: The substantiation here rested partly on the caregiver's handling of the children's medical and daycare appointments, and the Court held that shortfalls of that kind do not amount to abuse or neglect.
relevance.DEC-01: This case supplies the substantive definition that separates a report that should be closed or graded low from one that can be substantiated.
relevance.DEC-02: It describes the out-of-home abuse and neglect investigating team's authority under 22 M.R.S. §§ 4088 and 8101 and the preponderance standard that governs its findings.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the leading Maine authority on what a substantiated finding requires and on the liberty interest created by placement in the Department's database available to employers.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the paradigm Maine case of a court vacating an agency abuse finding for failure to meet the substantive standard.
relevance.FAIL-05: Because substantiation blocks employment and caregiving roles involving children, an erroneous finding operates as a de facto occupational bar that the Court treated as a liberty deprivation.
relevance.INP-09: The Court relied on the Department's own policy-manual revisions adding a severity element, showing how internal policy change follows external scrutiny.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation from complaint to formal investigation of a licensed caregiver is governed by the out-of-home investigating team statute discussed at length here.
relevance.PMC-06: The decision documents the stigma and tangible-burden consequences of database listing, the exact harms a registry-accountability analysis must measure.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: The First Circuit affirmed judgment for a Maine Department of Human Services caseworker and a Maine state trooper, holding that removing five children without a prior hearing violated neither substantive nor procedural due process where there was reasonable suspicion of abuse and ex parte judicial review within hours plus a hearing three business days later.
cases.quote: no substantive due process violation is stated if there existed a reasonable suspicion that abuse had occurred or that a threat of abuse was imminent at the time of removal

relevance.ACT-03: It is the First Circuit's Maine-specific benchmark for how quickly post-removal judicial review must follow placement of children in state custody.
relevance.DEC-04: This is the controlling circuit authority for a Maine emergency removal: reasonable suspicion of abuse or imminent abuse, followed by prompt ex parte review and a hearing within days.
relevance.FAIL-02: A wrongful-removal § 1983 claim in Maine must overcome both the reasonable-suspicion standard and qualified immunity as applied on these facts.
relevance.INP-03: The removal followed a state trooper's arrest of the father on assault charges involving the children, which is the classic law-enforcement referral pathway.
relevance.INP-12: Protective custody taken before any court order is constitutional where evidence of abuse or imminent danger exists and adequate post-removal process follows.

cases.case_name: Hatch v. Department for Children, Youth & Their Families
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: The First Circuit held that the Constitution allows a caseworker to take temporary custody of a child without a hearing on an objectively reasonable suspicion that abuse has occurred or is imminent, and affirmed because the information the caseworker had, including a school report and a physician's hold, met that standard.
cases.quote: Because the welfare of the child is paramount, an objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse justifies protective measures.

relevance.DEC-02: The court expressly rejected any requirement that a caseworker complete a full investigation and reach probable cause before acting.
relevance.DEC-03: The opinion explains that even a single instance of apparent abuse can support protective action, which informs how thin a record may support an agency finding.
relevance.DEC-04: This is the governing First Circuit standard for the emergency-removal decision that binds Maine caseworkers.
relevance.FAIL-02: A removal below the reasonable-suspicion floor is the circuit's definition of an unlawful removal actionable under § 1983.
relevance.INP-02: The court analyzed the reliability of a lay report under a totality-of-the-circumstances test drawn from Fourth Amendment reasonable-suspicion doctrine.
relevance.INP-03: It treats information relayed through school officials and police channels as usable if cloaked with indicia of reliability.
relevance.INP-06: The court held hearsay and tips may establish reasonable suspicion, with the required quantity of information varying inversely with the tip's reliability.
relevance.INP-08: The report originated with a school nurse's and teacher's observations relayed by the principal, the classic educational-disclosure trigger.
relevance.INP-12: It is the leading circuit authority on the constitutional floor for taking a child into temporary protective custody before a hearing.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: The First Circuit affirmed qualified immunity for child-welfare caseworkers sued for failing to protect twins abused in a licensed foster home, holding that even assuming a special relationship arose from foster placement, the plaintiffs must show conscience-shocking conduct and their evidence did not show even deliberate indifference.
cases.quote: Even then, the claim against the defendants must also involve "conscience-shocking" conduct by state officials

relevance.ACT-03: It sets the constitutional standard governing an agency's ongoing duty to monitor a child it has placed in foster care, including unreported adults in the home.
relevance.FAIL-04: This is the controlling circuit standard for failure-to-protect claims when a child is seriously harmed while under agency supervision.
relevance.OUT-06: Serious injury in foster care does not by itself generate liability; violations of state licensing regulations, even in bad faith, are not enough.
relevance.PMC-04: The court's framework explains why fatality and serious-injury reviews rarely translate into successful federal claims in this circuit.

cases.case_name: Connor B. ex rel. Vigurs v. Patrick
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: The First Circuit affirmed judgment for the state in a systemic foster-care class action, holding the record did not establish a class-wide substantive due process violation or a class-wide failure to maintain individualized case plans under the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act.
cases.quote: We agree with the district court that this record does not show a class-wide failure to provide documentation in the form of individualized case plans.

relevance.FAIL-03: It is the circuit's leading treatment of AACWA compliance litigation and of the Secretary of HHS's parallel power to withhold federal funds for substantial non-compliance.
relevance.FAIL-04: The court distinguished documented system deficiencies from constitutional violations, which is the barrier any systemic child-safety claim must clear.
relevance.INP-09: The opinion catalogues the kinds of systemic performance data that oversight bodies generate and explains why deficiencies alone do not establish liability.
relevance.OUT-04: Case plans under 42 U.S.C. § 675(1) are the federal vehicle for documenting a youth's services and steps toward permanency, including transition planning.
relevance.PMC-01: The court described the federal monitoring and funding-withholding mechanism as the primary enforcement route when a state underperforms.
relevance.PMC-02: It notes the roughly sixty million dollars in federal foster-care funding at stake, framing the financial leverage behind audit findings.
relevance.PMC-03: The decision redirects systemic child-welfare reform to the legislature and the executive rather than the courts, which is where citizen review panels operate.
relevance.PMC-04: Editorial findings of agency deficiency by a trial court, short of constitutional error, are directed to the political branches for correction.
relevance.PMC-06: The holding shows what quantum of cross-system evidence a systemic non-compliance claim must produce to survive in this circuit.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that before a State may irrevocably terminate parental rights, due process requires proof of its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence, and a preponderance standard is unconstitutional.
cases.quote: Thus, at a parental rights termination proceeding, a near-equal allocation of risk between the parents and the State is constitutionally intolerable.

relevance.OUT-02: This is the federal constitutional floor that 22 M.R.S. § 4055(1)(B)(2) implements, and the Court's footnote list of conforming states already included Maine's statute.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's requirement that a state plan provide for reasonable efforts to prevent removal and enable return creates no privately enforceable right, either implied under the Act or through 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.FAIL-03: It is the reason federal child-welfare compliance failures are ordinarily remedied through HHS funding leverage rather than private suit.
relevance.OUT-04: The same reasoning limits private enforcement of the title IV-E plan requirements that underwrite extended foster care and transition services.
relevance.PMC-01: The Court confined title IV-E state-plan requirements to a duty to have an approved plan, which is what CFSR review, not litigation, polices.
relevance.PMC-02: The enforcement mechanism the Court left intact is administrative and fiscal, which is why audit findings matter more than lawsuits here.
relevance.PMC-06: Any accountability analysis built on federal statutory requirements must account for the absence of a private right of action under this holding.

cases.holding: The Law Court vacated a temporary guardianship awarded to a grandmother, holding that the finding of a temporarily intolerable living situation was clearly erroneous because the overwhelming record evidence showed the mother was a fit parent at the time of the hearing.
cases.quote: Given the overwhelming record evidence that Nicole was a fit parent at the time of the hearing, the court's finding to the contrary is clearly erroneous

relevance.ACT-04: A relative caregiver cannot convert de facto care into legal custody without clear and convincing proof of the parent's current unfitness.
relevance.INP-05: When a relative petitions in Probate Court instead of triggering a child-protective report, the parent's fitness must still be assessed as of the hearing date, not on historical conduct.
relevance.OUT-03: This is the Maine case that disciplines the temporarily-intolerable-living-situation element, requiring current, not past, parental unfitness.
relevance.OUT-05: It is a working example of Maine appellate review reversing a custodial deprivation for insufficient evidence and returning the child to the parent.

cases.holding: The Law Court held that Maine's protection from abuse statute permits a court to award temporary parental rights and responsibilities to a nonparent who is a person responsible for the child, and that doing so on this record would not violate the biological father's due process rights.
cases.quote: granting temporary parental rights concerning Brant's son to Judy would not violate Brant's procedural due process rights

relevance.ACT-05: This is the Maine authority on the reach of a protection from abuse order as a child-safety instrument that can move custody without a child protection petition.
relevance.INP-05: A stepparent or other responsible adult may go directly to the PFA court for protective relief rather than routing the concern through the child-protective hotline.

cases.case_name: In re Child of Philip S.
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed dismissal for lack of standing of a de facto parentage complaint brought by the paternal uncle and aunt after the child was removed from their kinship placement and placed with a non-kinship foster family.
cases.quote: The special standing requirement acknowledges that a parent defending against such litigation inherently suffers an intrusion on parental rights.

relevance.ACT-03: The opinion shows the agency moving a child out of a kinship home into a non-kinship foster placement and the very limited legal recourse the former caregivers had.
relevance.ACT-04: Kinship caregivers in Maine must satisfy every element of the de facto parentage standing statute, 19-A M.R.S. § 1891, by a preponderance before they get a plenary hearing.

cases.case_name: In re Child of Taylor M.
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination of parental rights to an Indian child, holding the State complied with ICWA and the 2023 Maine Indian Child Welfare Act on the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt damage finding supported by a tribally designated qualified expert witness, on placement preferences, and on active efforts.
cases.quote: Thus, there is a dual burden of proof, one federal and one state, in a hearing on a petition for termination of parental rights as to an Indian child.

relevance.INP-11: This is the first Law Court decision applying MICWA, 22 M.R.S. §§ 3941-3957, alongside ICWA, including MICWA's definition of a qualified expert witness.
relevance.OUT-02: It confirms that state unfitness under 22 M.R.S. § 4055 must be independently proved by clear and convincing evidence even where the ICWA findings are satisfied.

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed some redactions and vacated others under the Freedom of Access Act, holding that FOAA exceptions are strictly construed, that the agency bears the burden of showing just and proper cause for withholding, and that material outside any statutory exception must be disclosed.
cases.quote: because no statutory exception applies to this redaction, we conclude that the officer's name in 0007 was not redacted for just and proper cause and must therefore be disclosed

relevance.DEC-03: The same personnel-records analysis governs whether a final written decision imposing discipline on a state child-welfare employee becomes public.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the Law Court's clearest recent statement that an agency withholding records bears the burden and that exceptions are read narrowly.
relevance.INP-09: Records of complaints that result in discipline become public once a final written decision imposes or upholds discipline, which is a practical oversight lever.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and misconduct material held by a Maine agency is presumptively public unless a specific confidentiality statute applies.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen oversight in Maine runs through 1 M.R.S. §§ 400-414 and the strict-construction rule applied here.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the governing Maine FOAA framework for a transparency request and for challenging redactions in Superior Court under 1 M.R.S. § 409(1).

cases.case_name: In re Children of Destiny H.
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed the termination judgment and the denial of the mother's Rule 60(b) ineffective-assistance motion, finding no due process violation, while prospectively enlarging the deadline for filing such motions from twenty-one to forty-two days after the appeal period expires.
cases.quote: We also cannot conclude that the court violated the mother's due process rights.

relevance.FAIL-01: This is the current Maine procedural framework for attacking a termination judgment on ineffective-assistance grounds, including the new forty-two day Rule 60(b) deadline and the affidavit requirements.

cases.case_name: In re Children of Shannevia Y.
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination of parental rights, holding the record generated no prima facie showing of ineffective assistance where counsel pursued a reasonable trial strategy and successfully obtained interested-person status for relatives proposed as permanency guardians.
cases.quote: The record therefore does not generate a prima facie showing that the mother's attorney's performance was deficient or undermines confidence in the result.

relevance.FAIL-01: It shows how the Law Court reviews an ineffective-assistance claim on the existing record, weighing reasonable trial strategy against the outcome.
relevance.OUT-03: The opinion illustrates the permanency guardianship alternative being litigated at the termination hearing and rejected on suitability findings about the grandmother and great-aunt.

cases.holding: The Law Court vacated judgment on the pleadings for a child protective caseworker, holding that where the complaint alleges she interviewed and physically examined a child at school without parental notice, acted beyond her statutory authority, and acted with malice, Maine Tort Claims Act immunity could not be resolved on the pleadings.
cases.quote: At a minimum, however, plaintiffs' complaint alleges that defendant acted beyond the bounds of any statutory authority she might have, and that she acted with malice.

relevance.ACT-06: The caseworker's physical examination of the child during a school interview is the conduct the Court held could fall outside her statutory authority.
relevance.DEC-01: The Department ultimately dismissed its own petition for insufficient evidence, the practical picture of a case that should have been closed earlier.
relevance.DEC-02: This is the Maine authority on the limits of investigative technique: interviewing a child not named in the referral, without parental notice and without grounds to believe notice would increase the threat of serious harm.
relevance.FAIL-02: The removal here followed a preliminary protection order the Department voluntarily dismissed for insufficient evidence, and the Court let the wrongful-conduct claims proceed.
relevance.FAIL-05: The complaint alleged the caseworker told neighbors, the Department of Education, and others that the abuse had been verified, and the Court held those defamation and civil-rights counts could not be dismissed on immunity grounds.
relevance.INP-01: It marks the line between protected discretionary investigative acts and conduct beyond statutory authority once a report is received.
relevance.INP-02: The investigation began from a third-party referral about a group of children and expanded to a child who had never been named in it.
relevance.INP-03: Two Maine State Troopers accompanied the caseworker to the family home, illustrating the joint law-enforcement and CPS interview posture.
relevance.INP-06: A referral naming other children does not authorize investigative action against a family never mentioned in the report.
relevance.INP-08: The interview and examination took place at the child's school without any notice to his mother and stepfather.
relevance.INP-10: Escalating from a general referral to targeted investigation of a specific household requires statutory authority, and exceeding it forfeits immunity.
relevance.OUT-05: The Department dismissed the preliminary child protection petition at the hearing for insufficient evidence and the child was returned home that same proceeding.

cases.case_name: In re Child of Rebecca R.
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination of both parents' rights, holding the father's ADA and Maine Human Rights Act accommodation claim was unpreserved because he never requested an accommodation and, in any event, the record supported the finding that his sleep pattern was a lifestyle choice rather than a disability, and that the mother's unfitness rested on far more than her inability to afford housing.
cases.quote: he did not request an accommodation under the ADA or MHRA and thus failed to preserve the issue for appeal

relevance.FAIL-05: This is the Maine authority on disability-discrimination and poverty-based challenges in termination proceedings, and it holds that an accommodation must be requested in the trial court to be reviewable.

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed appointment of the paternal grandparents as full guardians over the mother's objection, holding the Probate Court's findings that the mother was unfit and presented a temporarily intolerable living situation and that the appointment served the child's best interest satisfied 18-A M.R.S. §§ 5-204 and 5-207.
cases.quote: Here, there was no dispute as to venue or notice, and the court found all of the elements necessary to support a guardianship judgment pursuant to sections 5-204 and 5-207.

relevance.ACT-04: It is the working model of a kinship guardianship established with one parent's consent and over the other parent's objection.
relevance.INP-04: The guardianship ran alongside a District Court parental rights action, and the Probate Court expressly reserved review pending that case's disposition.
relevance.INP-05: A grandparent's guardianship petition is the private-law counterpart to a child-protective referral, and the consent of one legal custodian changes the proof required.
relevance.OUT-03: This case sets out the findings a Maine Probate Court must make to enter a permanent minor guardianship as a permanency outcome.

cases.case_name: In re Child of Christian D.
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination of the father's parental rights, holding the trial court's findings satisfied M.R. Civ. P. 52(a)'s requirement of specific, independently made findings and that it properly exercised its discretion in choosing adoption over a permanency guardianship.
cases.quote: the record supports the court's ultimate findings that termination of the father's parental rights and adoption are in the best interest of the child

relevance.OUT-02: This is the current statement of the Rule 52(a) specific-findings requirement in Maine termination judgments and of when a reviewing court may infer findings absent a Rule 52(b) motion.
relevance.OUT-03: It is the leading recent authority on the court's discretion to reject a permanency guardianship in favor of adoption where the child needs permanency now.

cases.case_name: In re Child of Barni A.
cases.holding: The Law Court vacated termination of a mother's rights to her medically fragile child and remanded, holding that where the Department never provided the 24/7 private duty nursing to which the child was legally entitled under MaineCare and never followed up on indications that the mother has an intellectual disability, the record did not establish her unfitness by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: We cannot assume that the mother would have been found unfit if the Department had met its legal obligations.

relevance.ACT-01: The services at issue were legally mandated benefits, not discretionary offerings, so the mother's inability to manage without them could not be charged against her.
relevance.ACT-02: The Court tied the Department's reunification obligation under 22 M.R.S. § 4041(1-A)(A)(1)(c)(iv) to services tailored to a parent who may have an intellectual disability.
relevance.ACT-06: The case turns on the child's entitlement to Level IV Private Duty Nursing under MaineCare and the Department's failure, as the program administrator, to supply it.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is the most significant recent Maine reversal of a termination judgment for agency failure, remanded with directions to explore alternatives to termination.
relevance.FAIL-03: The Department's default on a Medicaid-mandated service obligation was treated as legally significant to the child-protective outcome, not merely as a funding matter.
relevance.FAIL-05: The Court held that an undiagnosed intellectual disability the Department declined to investigate cannot be the unspoken basis of an unfitness finding.
relevance.INP-07: The child's complex medical needs and the nursing services required to meet them were the substance of the case from the outset.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification cannot be declared impossible where the agency itself withheld the legally required services that would make it possible.
relevance.OUT-02: Termination cannot rest on a parent's inability to do alone what the State was legally obligated to help her do.
relevance.PMC-01: The decision is a documented instance of a state agency's failure to deliver federally funded services driving a child-welfare outcome.

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed denial of relief from a final termination judgment and denial of intervention and interested-person status to a cousin couple and to an unrelated couple, holding that kinship-placement claims never raised during the termination proceeding were waived and that intervention requires a demonstrated special relationship with the child.
cases.quote: A special relationship with the child must be demonstrated.

relevance.ACT-04: Relatives who wish to be considered for kinship placement under 22 M.R.S. § 4062(4) must come forward during the protective proceeding, not after termination.
relevance.OUT-05: The opinion shows the child protection case being dismissed after termination and the narrow grounds on which a final judgment can be reopened under Rule 60(b).

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed the termination judgment and the denial of Rule 60(b)(6) relief, and in doing so established the process and standard for ineffective-assistance-of-counsel claims in Maine child protection cases: the claim may be raised on direct appeal where the record suffices, otherwise by a Rule 60(b)(6) motion filed within twenty-one days after the appeal period expires, in every instance supported by a signed and sworn affidavit, and judged by a Strickland-modeled test of deficient performance plus prejudice.
cases.quote: the parent making the claim must submit a signed and sworn affidavit stating, with specificity, the basis for the claim.

relevance.FAIL-01: This is the foundational Maine decision creating the route by which a parent can attack a termination judgment for counsel's failures, and it fixes both prerequisites the later cases apply — the Rule 60(b)(6) vehicle with its deadline (since enlarged to forty-two days by In re Children of Destiny H.) and the mandatory signed, sworn affidavit stating the basis of the claim with specificity.

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights, holding that incarceration gives a parent no reduced standard or 'pass' on parental responsibilities and that a parent who cannot meet the child's needs now and for the foreseeable future is unfit whatever the cause of that inability, while emphasizing that incarceration is one factor among many to be assessed case by case.
cases.quote: a parent who is unable to meet his child's needs—now and for the foreseeable future—is an unfit parent whose parental rights are subject to termination.

relevance.OUT-02: This is the actual source of Maine's incarceration-and-unfitness rule that In re Children of Matthew G. later quotes: the cause of the parental incapacity — mental illness, substance abuse, violence, incarceration or anything else — does not change the unfitness test, which turns on the parent's ability to meet the child's needs now and in the foreseeable future.

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination of the father's parental rights notwithstanding the Department's failure to develop and file the reunification plan that 22 M.R.S. § 4041 and the jeopardy order required, holding that the Department's section 4041 compliance is not a discrete element of proof in a termination proceeding and distinguishing In re Thomas D. because this father knew what rehabilitation was expected of him, was himself partly responsible for the plan's absence, and lost his rights for his inability to care for and protect his children rather than for failing undisclosed services.
cases.quote: although the Department's obligations pursuant to section 4041 are mandatory, the Department's failure to satisfy those obligations does not preclude a termination of parental rights.

relevance.ACT-02: This is the controlling counterweight to In re Thomas D. and In re Child of Barni A. on court-ordered service plans: the section 4041 plan duties are mandatory, but their breach is not a discrete element of proof and does not by itself defeat a termination, and the Court limits Thomas D. to cases where the parent was never told what services were required.
relevance.OUT-01: It marks the limit of the agency-default argument against a termination: where the parent knew what rehabilitation was needed and himself obstructed development of the plan, the absence of a filed reunification plan neither preserves reunification nor bars a finding of unfitness.

cases.holding: In a per curiam opinion the Law Court reached the merits of an otherwise moot jeopardy appeal under the collateral-consequences exception, because the jeopardy findings could be treated as an administrative substantiation of abuse affecting the mother's employment and her ability to care for other children, and then vacated the jeopardy order for insufficient evidence and remanded with direction to dismiss the child protection proceedings.
cases.quote: Because of these collateral consequences, we reach the merits of the appeal.

relevance.DEC-03: This is the Law Court's explanation of why a judicial jeopardy finding matters beyond the protective case: the findings may be interpreted as a substantiation of abuse in the Department's administrative proceedings, with consequences for employment and for caring for children other than the parent's own.
relevance.OUT-04: It is the decision that actually recognizes the collateral-consequences exception permitting review of a jeopardy order after the child has turned eighteen during the appeal, the point for which In re Nicholas S. is usually cited.
relevance.OUT-05: The Court vacated the jeopardy order and its supporting findings for insufficient evidence and directed the District Court to dismiss the child protection proceedings outright.

cases.case_name: In re Children of Troy H.
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed a jeopardy order as to two Indian children, holding that Maine law and ICWA apply concurrently to produce a dual burden of proof — preponderance of the evidence for jeopardy under 22 M.R.S. § 4035(2) and clear and convincing evidence for ICWA's likely-serious-damage finding under 25 U.S.C. § 1912(e) — and that the trial court's unchallenged findings of the father's physical response to the children supported jeopardy.
cases.quote: We note initially that Maine law and federal law apply concurrently to this proceeding, resulting in a "dual burden of proof."

relevance.INP-11: This is the Law Court's own statement that state law and ICWA operate concurrently once a case is identified as involving an Indian child, and it is the authority In re Child of Taylor M. cites for the dual-burden sentence the brief quotes from that case.
relevance.DEC-05: It sets out precisely what the Department must carry at a contested adjudication involving an Indian child: preponderance of the evidence on jeopardy under 22 M.R.S. § 4035(2), plus ICWA's separate clear and convincing showing under 25 U.S.C. § 1912(e).

cases.case_name: Maureen D. Davis v. Bennie C. McGuire III
cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed dismissal of a grandmother's de facto parentage complaint for lack of standing, holding that a single standard of proof governs the standing determination under 19-A M.R.S. § 1891 — a burden of persuasion, not mere production — so that the petitioner must prove every statutory element of a de facto parent relationship by a preponderance of the evidence whether the court decides standing on the affidavits or after a hearing.
cases.quote: a petitioner must prove each of the elements of a de facto parent relationship with the child by—as we now hold—a preponderance of the evidence.

relevance.ACT-04: This is the decision that established the standing burden In re Child of Philip S. applies to kinship caregivers: a relative must prove every element of 19-A M.R.S. § 1891(3) by a preponderance before any plenary de facto parentage hearing is available.
relevance.INP-05: A relative or long-term caregiver who seeks legal status outside the child-protective system must first clear a standing threshold the Court designed to protect the parent from the constitutional intrusion of having to defend the claim at all.

cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed with modifications a minor guardianship granted to the maternal grandmother over the father's objection, construing the 'temporarily intolerable living situation' element of 18-A M.R.S. § 5-204(c) to require proof of parental unfitness — that the parent is currently unable to meet the child's needs with an effect on the child's well-being that may be dramatic or even traumatic — together with a finding that the proposed guardian will provide a living situation in the child's best interest, and striking one finding unsupported by the evidence.
cases.quote: proof of parental unfitness is a required element to support the establishment of a guardianship over the parent's objection.

relevance.OUT-03: This is the Law Court's framework decision construing 18-A M.R.S. § 5-204(c), supplying the two-part test — current parental inability with a dramatic or traumatic effect on the child, plus a best-interest finding as to the proposed guardian — that Guardianship of Ella M. Grenier and the later minor-guardianship cases apply.
relevance.INP-05: When a grandparent or other caregiver petitions in Probate Court rather than making a child-protective report, this case states what the petitioner must establish before the parent may be displaced, on a standard the Court describes as less stringent than jeopardy but still requiring unfitness.

cases.case_name: Blethen Maine Newspapers, Inc. v. State
cases.holding: The Law Court held that the Attorney General's investigative records concerning sexual abuse allegations against eighteen deceased priests must be disclosed under the Freedom of Access Act because the substantial public interest in knowing how the government handled those allegations outweighed the remaining personal privacy interests, but vacated and remanded so the records would first be redacted to remove the names and identifying information of living persons.
cases.quote: An informed citizenry has no less of an interest in information that might document governmental efficiency or effectiveness than it does in information documenting governmental negligence or malfeasance.

relevance.FAIL-06: The Court rejected a blanket privacy-based refusal to release a prosecutor's file on child sexual-abuse allegations and ordered disclosure subject to redaction, holding that the public's interest in FOAA records is not confined to proof of government wrongdoing.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the leading Law Court FOAA decision on public access to government records about the handling of child sexual-abuse allegations, and it gives a transparency request a broader and less easily distinguished footing than a personnel-records case such as Anctil.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court affirmed judgment for county social services officials, holding that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative constitutional duty on a State to protect a child from private violence — even where the agency received repeated reports, opened a file and monitored the home — because the affirmative duty to protect arises only from a state-imposed restraint on the individual's own freedom to act, not from the State's knowledge of the danger or its expressed intention to help.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.FAIL-04: This is the controlling federal baseline for every failure-to-protect claim against a child-welfare agency, and the source of the special-relationship and custodial-restraint framework that J.R. v. Gloria applies in the First Circuit; absent custody, agency knowledge of the danger creates no constitutional duty.
relevance.OUT-06: A child's catastrophic injury after repeated agency contact does not by itself state a constitutional claim, which is why Maine serious-injury and fatality cases proceed, if at all, on the narrow custodial special-relationship theory the Court reserved for children placed by the State in foster homes.

notes: Maine has no intermediate appellate court. All state authority here is from the Supreme Judicial Court of Maine sitting as the Law Court (court_id 'me'), which hears child protection appeals directly from the District Court under 22 M.R.S. Sec. 4006. Every case listed was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its opinion text read; no case is cited from memory. All quotes were verified programmatically as exact substrings of the retrieved opinion text after whitespace and curly-quote normalization.

Every quote is from a majority or single-authored lead opinion. No syllabus, headnote, dissent or concurrence text was used. Where a Law Court opinion stated a rule only by quoting an earlier decision (e.g. the Jewel I/Jewel II formulations in Guardianship of Ella M. Grenier, or the In re Alijah K. incarceration formulation in In re Children of Matthew G.), that quoted language was deliberately avoided in favour of the deciding court's own sentence.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the ME node files are keyword-matched noise. Of the recurring titles, only In re Child of Barni A., In re Child of Christian D., In re Child of Taylor M., In re Children of Destiny H., In re Children of Shannevia Y. and In re Child of Rebecca R. were retrieved, read and found on point; they are included here with verified citations. 'Doe v. Burnham', 'Doe v. Costin', 'In re William B. Blaisdell IV', 'In re Children of Billie S.', 'TPR, Inc. v. Paychex, Inc.', 'In re Involuntary Commitment of M.', 'In re Adult Guardianship of L.' and the adult-guardianship/adoption entries are either unrelated to child welfare or were not verifiable as on-point and were dropped.

NO MAINE AUTHORITY FOUND, OUT-04 (Extended Foster Care / Aging Out): repeated CourtListener searches of the Law Court for 22 M.R.S. Sec. 4037-A, extended care past 18, Chafee/independent-living, and young-adult voluntary agreements returned nothing on point. OUT-04 is therefore mapped to In re Nicholas S. and now In re Ciara H. (collateral-consequences exception lets the Law Court reach a jeopardy appeal even after the child turns eighteen), Suter v. Artist M. (no private enforcement of the title IV-E plan requirements that underwrite extended care) and Connor B. (AACWA case-plan documentation). A lawyer should treat 22 M.R.S. Sec. 4037-A as substantially untested in the Law Court.

NO MAINE AUTHORITY FOUND, DEC-06 (Differential / Alternative Response): Maine's statute grades findings three ways (unsubstantiated, indicated, substantiated) rather than operating a formal differential-response track, and no Law Court decision construes an alternative-response pathway. DEC-06 is mapped to the closest structural authorities (In re Thomas D. on the plan requirement, Adoption of Riahleigh M. on the absence of any constitutional service entitlement outside a Department case, In re B.C. on when the service track ends).

THIN AUTHORITY, DEC-01 (Screen-Out / Unfounded at Intake) and INP-09/PMC-01 through PMC-06: there is no Maine decision reviewing an intake screening decision or a CFSR, OIG, citizen-review-panel or fatality-commission determination. Those nodes are served by the closest analogues actually retrieved: Kane (what 'abuse or neglect' must mean before a finding can be made), John Doe v. DHHS (the error rate in unreviewed substantiations and the void-rule holding), Anctil, Blethen and In re Bailey M. (the FOAA and Sec. 4007/4008 confidentiality framework that governs any oversight records request), and Connor B. and Suter (federal monitoring and funding leverage as the operative enforcement mechanism rather than private litigation).

NO MAINE AUTHORITY FOUND, FAIL-04 / OUT-06 (child death or serious injury under agency supervision): searches for wrongful-death, negligent-supervision and duty-of-care claims against the Department produced no Law Court decision on the merits of such a claim. Huff v. Williams supplies the Maine Tort Claims Act discretionary-immunity bar that in practice forecloses those claims; DeShaney supplies the controlling federal constitutional baseline and J.R. v. Gloria the First Circuit's conscience-shocking standard for the federal substantive-due-process alternative. In re Bailey M. arises out of an actual death of a child in a Maine foster home but decides only the closure question.

No unpublished memorandum decisions were used. In re David H., 2009 ME 131, is a published opinion that follows an earlier unpublished memorandum affirmance (Mem-08-127) in the same matter; only the published 2009 opinion is relied on here.

In re Child of Barni A., 2024 ME 16, exists on CourtListener in both an original (cluster 9471586, opinion 9929424) and a revised (cluster 10376975, revised March 7, 2024) version. The text read and quoted is the original; counsel should check the revised opinion before quoting in a filing. The same duplication exists for In re Children of Destiny H. and In re Child of Taylor M.; the cluster ids given here are the ones whose opinion text was actually retrieved.

Citation form follows Maine's public-domain citation (e.g. 2018 ME 164, 198 A.3d 782). Where the CourtListener cluster carried no A.3d parallel cite (In re Child of Taylor M., In re Children of Destiny H., In re Children of Shannevia Y., In re Child of Rebecca R., In re Child of Christian D., In re Child of Barni A., In re Children of Troy H.), only the public-domain cite is given rather than a parallel cite that could not be verified from the cluster record. In re Child of Stephen E. is given as 2018 ME 71, 186 A.3d 134; the cluster carried only the A.3d cite, and the public-domain cite was confirmed from the Law Court's own citation of the case in In re Children of Matthew G.

Two practice points a Maine practitioner should carry away. First, under In re B.C. a cease-reunification order is interlocutory and unreviewable; the only appellate handle is a sufficiency challenge to the underlying aggravating-factor finding embedded in the jeopardy order. Second, under In re Children of Destiny H. the deadline for a Rule 60(b) ineffective-assistance motion is now forty-two days after the notice-of-appeal deadline expires, not the twenty-one days fixed by In re M.P., and the parent's own signed and sworn affidavit remains mandatory in every case (In re M.P.; In re Children of Matthew G.; In re Child of Stephen E.).

Maine enacted its own Maine Indian Child Welfare Act (22 M.R.S. Secs. 3941-3957) in 2023. In re Child of Taylor M., 2025 ME 7, is the first Law Court decision applying it and should be read together with In re Children of Troy H. (2019), In re Child of Radience K. (2019) and In re Annette P. (1991), which remain the sources of the dual-burden framework and of the clear-and-convincing standard for ICWA active efforts in Maine.

Fourth Amendment and Section 1983 authority is First Circuit (Hatch, Tower, J.R. v. Gloria, Connor B.) resting on the U.S. Supreme Court baseline in DeShaney, which binds federal courts in the District of Maine. Tower v. Leslie-Brown arises from Maine facts and is the most directly applicable removal-timing authority. No Law Court decision squarely addresses warrantless caseworker entry into a home or the seizure of a child at school under the Fourth Amendment; Cunningham v. Haza (1988) is the closest state analogue and reaches the question only as a Maine Tort Claims Act immunity issue on the pleadings.

Added In re M.P., 2015 ME 138, 126 A.3d 718 (cluster 3150587) for FAIL-01: it is the foundational Law Court decision creating Maine's ineffective-assistance framework in child protection cases — the direct-appeal and Rule 60(b)(6) routes, the twenty-one day deadline later enlarged by In re Children of Destiny H., the mandatory signed and sworn affidavit, and the modified Strickland deficiency-plus-prejudice test — which Stephen E., Destiny H., Matthew G. and Shannevia Y. merely apply. To keep FAIL-01 within the six-case ceiling, In re Children of Shannevia Y. (cluster 9469703) was moved off FAIL-01; it remains mapped at OUT-03 and its case entry is unchanged.

Added In re Alijah K., 2016 ME 137, 147 A.3d 1159 (cluster 4252365) for OUT-02: it is the actual source of Maine's incarceration-and-unfitness rule that In re Children of Matthew G. quotes, holding that incarceration confers no reduced standard and that the test is whether the parent can meet the child's needs now and for the foreseeable future. To keep OUT-02 within the six-case ceiling, In re Child of Taylor M. (cluster 10340240) was moved off OUT-02; it remains mapped at INP-11 and its case entry is unchanged.

Added In re Doris G., 2006 ME 142, 912 A.2d 572 (cluster 5142769) for ACT-02 and OUT-01: it is the controlling counterweight to In re Thomas D. and In re Child of Barni A., holding that the Department's mandatory section 4041 plan duties are not a discrete element of proof and that agency default does not preclude a finding of unfitness where the parent knew what rehabilitation was required and himself obstructed the plan. Without it the brief was materially one-sided on the consequences of agency default.

Added In re Ciara H., 2011 ME 109, 30 A.3d 835 (cluster 2321355) for DEC-03, OUT-04 and OUT-05: it is the per curiam decision that actually recognizes the collateral-consequences exception (a jeopardy finding may be read as an administrative substitution of abuse affecting employment and care of other children) for which In re Nicholas S. is usually cited, and it vacated the jeopardy order for insufficient evidence with direction to dismiss the proceedings.

Added In re Children of Troy H., 2019 ME 154 (cluster 4674694) for INP-11 and DEC-05: it is the Law Court's own statement that Maine law and ICWA apply concurrently to produce a dual burden of proof (preponderance for jeopardy under 22 M.R.S. Sec. 4035(2); clear and convincing evidence under 25 U.S.C. Sec. 1912(e)), and it is the authority In re Child of Taylor M. cites for the dual-burden sentence quoted from that case. Note that Troy H. is a jeopardy rather than a termination appeal; the CourtListener cluster carries no A.3d parallel cite, so only the public-domain cite is given.

Added Maureen D. Davis v. Bennie C. McGuire III, 2018 ME 72, 186 A.3d 837 (cluster 4500792) for ACT-04 and INP-05: it established the standing burden under 19-A M.R.S. Sec. 1891 on which In re Child of Philip S. expressly rests, holding that a single standard of persuasion governs and the petitioner must prove every element of a de facto parent relationship by a preponderance whether standing is decided on the affidavits or after a hearing. The case is styled by the Law Court with the parties' full names, which is how case_name is given.

Added Guardianship of Jewel M., 2010 ME 17, 989 A.2d 726 (cluster 1995678) for OUT-03 and INP-05: it is the Law Court's framework decision construing the 'temporarily intolerable living situation' element of 18-A M.R.S. Sec. 5-204(c) to require proof of current parental unfitness plus a best-interest finding as to the proposed guardian, and it supplies the formulations Guardianship of Ella M. Grenier applies. A second Jewel M. opinion in the same matter (2010 ME 80, 2 A.3d 301, cluster 2443833) appeared in the search results and was not relied on; the framework decision is the March 2010 opinion.

Added Blethen Maine Newspapers, Inc. v. State, 2005 ME 56, 871 A.2d 523 (cluster 2180233) for FAIL-06 and PMC-05: it is a leading Law Court Freedom of Access Act decision ordering disclosure, subject to redaction, of a prosecutor's investigative file on child sexual-abuse allegations, and it gives the transparency analysis a broader footing than Anctil's personnel-records holding. Counsel should note the split: the opinion of the Court was authored by Levy, J., joined by Dana and Calkins, JJ., with the Chief Justice concurring separately and three justices dissenting; the quoted sentence is from the Court's opinion, not from the concurrence or either dissent.

Added DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services, 489 U.S. 189 (1989) (cluster 112202) for FAIL-04 and OUT-06: it is the controlling federal constitutional baseline from which every special-relationship and affirmative-duty proposition the brief draws from J.R. v. Gloria derives, and no failure-to-protect or serious-injury analysis is complete without it. The quote is from the opinion of the Court by Chief Justice Rehnquist, not from the syllabus or either dissent.

Coverage check for this pass: after the nine additions, every one of the 42 nodes is mapped to between two and six cases, and no node was found with fewer than two cases before the additions were made, so no further gap-filling search was required beyond the named authorities. The brief now carries 45 distinct cases, slightly above the 20-40 target, because the verifier's list of leading authorities was added in full rather than trimmed.

Authorities that could not be verified in this session: none of the nine named authorities failed verification — all nine were located on CourtListener, their clusters and opinion texts retrieved, and their quotes confirmed as exact substrings. The only partial failure is bibliographic: the A.3d parallel citation 218 A.3d 750 given for In re Children of Troy H. does not appear in the CourtListener cluster's citation record and is therefore omitted rather than reproduced unverified.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Daniel C., 480 A.2d 766 (Me. 1984) — the origin of the rule that the Department's reunification efforts are 'not a discrete element of proof in termination proceedings,' quoted and relied on by In re Doris G.; it is the root authority for ACT-02 and OUT-01 and the brief cites only its descendant. (Citation confirmed from the Doris G. opinion text.)

Missing (for a later pass): In re Denice F., 658 A.2d 1070 (Me. 1995) — the source of the Maine/ICWA 'dual burden of proof' formulation that In re Children of Troy H. and In re Child of Taylor M. both quote; INP-11 and DEC-05 currently cite only the cases that borrow it. (Citation confirmed from the Troy H. opinion text.)

Missing (for a later pass): Guardianship of Jeremiah T., 2009 ME 74, 976 A.2d 955 — the decision that first held proof of parental unfitness is a required element for a minor guardianship over a parent's objection; Guardianship of Jewel M. states the rule with an 'Id.' cite to it, and Chamberlain, Grenier and Gabriel Johnson all sit downstream of it. Missing from OUT-03 and INP-05. (Citation confirmed on CourtListener.)

Missing (for a later pass): In re Cody T., 2009 ME 95, 979 A.2d 81 — the incarcerated-parent decision that In re Alijah K. distinguishes in the very passage the brief quotes ('neither In re Cody T. nor any other authority gives a parent a "pass"'); a practitioner briefing OUT-02 for an incarcerated parent needs the case being limited, not only the limiting case. (Citation confirmed on CourtListener.)

Missing (for a later pass): Rideout v. Riendeau, 2000 ME 198, 761 A.2d 291 — the Law Court's leading constitutional decision on when a third party may obtain court-ordered access to a child over a fit parent's objection; it is the constitutional backdrop for the entire INP-05/ACT-04/OUT-03 private-caregiver line and is absent. (Citation confirmed on CourtListener.)

Missing (for a later pass): Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) — the federal constitutional baseline for the presumption that a fit parent acts in the child's best interest, which every Maine third-party guardianship and de facto parentage case in this brief presupposes; the brief supplies Santosky for the termination standard but nothing for the fit-parent presumption.
